en_summary: Some takeaways from this report. $60B of new AI orders in 13 weeks. $132B backlog. Full year raised by $10B. And every order "rigorously vetted for customer quality and access to capital, land and power." That's Dell directly answering the circular financing fear. Demand strong enough that you can turn away unvetted buyers is not what a bubble top looks like. Q4 EPS guides down sequentially on rising component costs, and inventory nearly tripled to feed the backlog. Great quarter, tougher margin road ahead. Bigger picture, Dell is the backbone of this buildout. They assemble the racks, test them, and stand them up. The backbone says demand is accelerating across 7,500+ customers, so everything downstream of those racks eventually gets its piece. Connectivity, power, cooling, all of it.

Nvidia's GPUs and the custom chips from Broadcom, Google and Amazon are mostly built at TSMC. AMD $AMD just got its first Helios rack running inside a Microsoft Azure lab, and the stock still broke below $400.

AMD says Microsoft accepted delivery this fall, powered up its first Helios rackscale system, and reports it is successfully running early workloads in validation. Azure plans to deploy Helios at scale and is expected to be among the first clouds to put it to work on AI inference. Per Microsoft, each liquid-cooled rack packs 72 MI455X GPUs, 18 EPYC "Venice" CPUs and 31 TB of HBM4.

Why it matters: Helios is AMD's answer to Nvidia's rack scale systems, and a hyperscaler running real workloads on it is the proof point the second half ramp needs. But this is a lab, not a customer deployment. No rack counts or financial terms were shared.

The tape did not care. AMD traded as low as $396 Tuesday, its first time under $400 since May and roughly 40% below its $649.42 high on Oct. 6, as the whole AI basket gave back Monday's Nvidia rally. A Monday shelf registration is also adding to the nerves: it reportedly covers about 337 million shares for resale, including roughly 160 million each tied to the OpenAI and Meta warrants, so investors are doing dilution math on the biggest AI deals in the company's history. Registered shares are not shares sold, and AMD gets no proceeds from resale, per reports.

Management expects $45M in annual benefits. Q3 free cash flow $170M.
text:
Beyond Warren Buffett buying shares of $TPL as a teenager in the 1940s, Murray Stahl of Horizon Kinetics discovered the company nearly five decades later.

Murray Stahl's first report for his new research service Horizon was about Texas Pacific Land $TPL and over several decades he built a position in the company that made him the largest shareholder. 

We came across Murray and TPL because he or his firm would constantly buy shares on the open market, often times just a few shares a day. 

The P symbols you see on the chart below are some of those purchases. 

I know at least two investment managers who had a chance to work directly with Murray and had nothing but nice things to say about him. 

He passed away earlier this year, the insider purchases stopped a few weeks ago and $3 billion acquisition of EagleRock Land $EROK was announced yesterday.

As I looked at the deal announcement come through, a thought crossed my mind: What would Murray think about this decision?

Hopefully we will explore the answer to that question in our next Merger Arbitrage Mondays article, unless we see a more interesting deal or a pre-deal situation come through by the end of this holiday shortened week.

Kohl’s (KSS) is surging +16.6% to $24.73 following a Q3 FY26 earnings beat and raised guidance this morning, putting it just pennies below its $25.00 Call Wall.

Post-Earnings IV Crush & Skew: 1-month implied volatility sits at 80.92% (IV Rank 63.26%) with a $1.08 implied move, and Skew Rank is elevated at 96.00% as traders aggressively bid up upside calls following the beat.

$SPX — Weekly Elliott Wave Update

This is for those who have actually read and studied the Elliott Wave Principle, not those who Google a few images and try to force a wave count onto a chart.

I have two valid wave counts here.

Scenario 1: We completed five waves within Wave (3), reaching the 100% Fibonacci relationship, and are now in the higher-degree Orange Wave (4).

The first leg down was Wave A. We could spend the remainder of 2026 chopping around in Wave B before another leg down in Wave C next year.

Scenario 2: We are still in Wave 4 of the diagonal. If price manages to squeeze out one more high, the higher-degree Orange Wave (4) comes into play next year.

Looking at the number of weekly SELL signals and downswings across the market, Scenario 1 makes more sense to me right now.

I need to see new demand and a weekly BUY signal before entertaining Scenario 2.

The tricky part is determining which degree of Wave 4 we are currently in.

I will track both counts every week. No need to waste too much time debating wave counts or forcing a bullish or bearish narrative.

As price gives me more clarity, I will adjust my wave count accordingly.

Swings and signals will dictate my execution, not the wave count.

Let price do the talking.
